title: Monic reduction forces monicity for a commuting idempotent determinant
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(A)$ an ideal, and $T,P\in\operatorname{Mat}_J(A)$ for a finite set $J$. Assume $P^2=P$, $TP=PT$, and the reduction of $D(T,P)$ [def-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly] in $(A/I)[X]$ is monic. Then $D(T,P)$ is monic.

source.place: Tag 09XI, lemma-characterize-henselian-pair, proof of (3) implies (1), splitting and characteristic-polynomial paragraphs; matrix formula and omitted details written out by G2

proof.text: The identities P²=P and P+(1-P)=1 give a split decomposition of A^J into the images of P and 1-P. Both are finite projective. Obtain finite standard free covers for both and refine to their product cover so both summands have bases.

T preserves both images because TP=PT. In their concatenated local basis P is diag(1,0), T is block diagonal, and 1-P+(X-T)P is diag(X-T_image,1). Its determinant is the ordinary characteristic polynomial on the image of P, monic of its local rank. Determinant invariance under conjugation and determinant base change justify these comparisons.

If A is nonzero, A/I is nonzero since I is in the Jacobson radical. Let d be the degree of the monic reduction. At every prime containing I, reduce the local determinant to the residue field. Degree preservation of the monic reduction and of the local monic determinant show that the image of P has rank d there. Its rank is locally constant. The closed locus where the rank differs from d, if nonempty, contains a maximal ideal. Every maximal ideal contains I, giving a contradiction. The rank is consequently d everywhere.

On each nonzero localization of the standard cover the determinant therefore has coefficient 1 at degree d and zero coefficients above d; these same equations hold on zero localizations. Injectivity on a standard cover gives these equations over A. They imply monicity. When A is zero its only polynomial is monic.
